assumptions: you have material worth packaging — exercises with answer keys, not an introduction to prompts
an audience that will pay for execution rather than information, which is the whole bet
a maintenance rhythm for tool guidance, since a stale curriculum is worse than none in this domain
clone_cost.estimate: days for the platform shell; the curriculum and the evidence are the months
clone_cost.why: A content library, a template store and accounts are ordinary work, and nothing described needs FastAPI and Firestore and Streamlit and Node at once. What takes months is repeatable exercises that reliably leave a non-technical person with something deployed, and someone keeping the model and API guidance current as the ecosystem the page itself calls overwhelming turns over.

hazard_note_absent: No regulated-outcome claim: nothing here asserts credentials, employment results or exam outcomes, so no hazard flag is raised. The relevant caution is for whoever copies the framing — promising published books and deployable systems without measuring a single learner is a marketing surface, and the exposure sits with the buyer, not with a reader of this record.

prior_art.relation: both serve a non-technical user who wants the finished artifact rather than the skill, and the contrast is about commitment: SketchWish names one output, discloses its caps and costs, and can be opened and tried; this promises five kinds of output and links nothing a reader can try.
both sell time saved; Greenlight states a measured before/after with a cost per run, which is the shape of claim this page's 'save measurable time' principle asks for and does not make.

what_breaks_first: Every claim about effectiveness, immediately, because there is nothing to break gracefully — no cohort size, no completion rate, no hours saved, no named organisation that onboarded. Second: the product boundary. A course, a template library and a hosted automation workspace have different failure modes, different owners and different prices, and the page does not say which of the three it is; the eleven Built With tags span two backend frameworks, two hosting stacks, two storage engines and two front-end approaches, which reads as the tool list a student touches across a year rather than the stack one service runs on.
what_to_steal: Segment a curriculum by the artifact the learner leaves with — a deployed workflow, a published book, a live dashboard — rather than by topic, because each module then has a one-question success test: did this produce a thing. And name the barrier concretely (API sprawl, coding environments, model selection, an ecosystem that changes monthly) instead of 'practical AI skills': that list is a usable brief for what a first session must hide.
worth_note: The genre is crowded and this entry is indistinguishable from it: practical application rather than theory, a list of output types, a stated tension between too simple and too technical. What would move it off this label is a single number from a real cohort, and the page itself names which number — people learn faster when they can automate something useful, publish a real result or save measurable time. The record is held for the absence of the measurement it argues for, not for the aim, which is a good one.
